summary: Provides an LDAP extended operation, Who am I?, letting a client learn the authorization identity the server has associated with it. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A way to ask the server who do you think I am right now, in case you are logged in as someone else.

questions: what is the ldap who am i operation
how does an ldap client find its authorization identity
what is an authzid in ldap
what is the oid for ldap whoami
subtitle: An LDAP extended operation that lets a client ask the server which authorization identity it currently associates with that client.

tldr.problem: After authenticating, an LDAP client may need to learn which identity the server actually treats it as. The earlier bind-control mechanism is not protected by the security layers that the Bind itself sets up.
tldr.mechanism: The 'Who am I?' extended operation uses the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3. The request has no value, and the response carries the authzId, or an empty value for an anonymous client.
tldr.outcome: It is intended to replace the Authorization Identity Controls of RFC 3829, and an extended operation sent after a Bind is protected by the security layers that Bind established.

today: RFC 4532 is a Proposed Standard from June 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is intended to replace the bind-control mechanism of RFC 3829.

sections.title: Why Ask Who You Are
sections.content:
The Who am I? operation lets an LDAP client obtain the primary authorization identity, in its primary form, that the server has associated with the user or application. Servers often associate several authorization identities with a client, and each may be written as several authzId strings, so the operation returns the one the server considers primary.

The RFC is meant to replace the Authorization Identity Controls in RFC 3829. Those use Bind request and response controls, and Bind controls are not protected by the security layers the Bind operation establishes. An extended operation sent after a Bind is protected by those layers, which is often what deployers want.

It is also useful separately from a Bind. It can be combined with the Proxied Authorization Control (RFC 4370) to learn the identity the server associates with an asserted identity, and it can be used before the Bind operation.
sections.eli5: Instead of tucking the question inside the login message, where it is not locked up safely, you ask it afterward over the secure line you just built.

sections.title: The Request and Response
sections.content:
The operation is an LDAP Extended Operation (RFC 4511) identified by the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3, called whoamiOID.

The whoami request is an ExtendedRequest whose requestName holds whoamiOID and whose requestValue is absent. The RFC gives a hex encoding of an example request.

The whoami response is an ExtendedResponse where responseName is absent and the response field, if present, is either empty or an authzId (RFC 4513). The RFC's example returns the authzId u:xxyyz@EXAMPLE.NET.
sections.eli5: The question is a blank form with just the operation's number on it. The answer is a short note with a name on it, or a blank note.

sections.title: How the Server Answers
sections.content:
Servers announce support by listing whoamiOID as a value of the supportedExtension attribute in their root DSE. A server SHOULD advertise it only when the client is willing and able to perform the operation.

If the server is willing and able, it SHALL return a response with a success resultCode. For an anonymous client the response field is present but empty. Otherwise it holds the authzId the server currently associates with the client.

If the server is unwilling or unable, it SHALL return an appropriate non-success resultCode (such as operationsError, protocolError, confidentialityRequired, insufficientAccessRights, busy, unavailable or unwillingToPerform) with the response field absent.

Clients MUST NOT invoke the operation while any Bind is in progress, including between two Bind requests of a multi-stage Bind. A server that receives such a request should return an operationsError result.
sections.eli5: If the server is happy to tell you, it says your name, or says nothing if you are a stranger. If it will not or cannot tell you, it answers with an error. And you must not ask in the middle of logging in.

sections.title: Extending with Controls
sections.content:
Future specifications may extend the operation with LDAP controls. When controls are attached, the operation reports the identity the server associates with the client in the context those controls indicate.

The RFC's worked example is the Proxied Authorization Control (RFC 4370), which asks that an operation run under an assumed identity. Because servers often map the asserted authzId to another identity, it is useful to ask for the authzId the server really uses. With that control attached, the operation returns the authzId the server associates with the asserted identity. The authorizationDenied (123) result code signals that the server does not allow the client to assume it.
sections.eli5: You can add a sticky note saying 'pretend I am Sam' and then ask who the desk thinks you are. If you are not allowed to be Sam, it says no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Identities associated with users may be sensitive. When they are, security layers should be established to protect them, and this mechanism is designed so that layers established by a Bind can protect the integrity and confidentiality of the authorization identity.

Servers may restrict the operation with access control or other limits, and the general LDAP security considerations in RFC 4510 apply.
sections.eli5: Who you are can be private, so the answer should travel inside the locked tunnel set up when you logged in.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3 was assigned by the OpenLDAP Foundation under its IANA-assigned private enterprise allocation. The IANA has registered it as an LDAP protocol mechanism with the description 'Who am I?' and the usage 'Extended Operation', with the IESG as change controller.
sections.eli5: The operation's number is written in an official public list so everyone agrees what it means.

messages.note: Success: authzId, or empty if anonymous. Otherwise a non-success resultCode with no response field.
